Matching CVEs

Source: vendor security advisories (NVD + vendor CNA feeds), CISA KEV catalog. Counts exclude third-party/disputed/no-impact CVEs. Generated from the CVE tracker store — a point-in-time snapshot; re-render after each refresh to update.

Methodology & Definitions

Scope & Sources

Data sources. CVEs are enumerated from the NVD CVE API filtered to each vendor TWO ways - by CPE vendor (cpe:2.3:*:<vendor>:*) AND by the vendor PSIRT's CNA (sourceIdentifier) - so freshly-disclosed CVEs that NVD has not yet attached product (CPE) data to are still caught. Each CVE is then enriched from the vendor's OWN record for product names, fixed builds and severity: Palo Alto and Check Point from the CVE-5.0 record (cveawg.mitre.org), Fortinet and Cisco from their CSAF (FortiGuard PSIRT / Cisco openVuln). Check Point severity additionally comes from its SK advisory page. Disclosure timelines come from the crediting researcher's write-up.

Products in scope. Enterprise SECURITY products only. Focused-security vendors (Check Point, Palo Alto, Fortinet, SonicWall, Sophos) are in scope by default. Broad-portfolio vendors (Cisco, Juniper) count ONLY their security lines - routers/switch OS (IOS, IOS XE, NX-OS, Catalyst/Nexus switches), compute (UCS), and collaboration (Webex, IP phones, contact center) are excluded.

Switches & access points. Network switches and Wi-Fi access points (e.g. FortiSwitch, FortiAP, Aironet, SonicWave) are network plumbing, not security products, and are excluded - UNLESS the same advisory also affects a firewall/gateway (the device acting as a security enforcement point), in which case the CVE is kept via that product.

Consumer lines. Consumer / personal-use products (e.g. Check Point ZoneAlarm) are excluded when they are the ONLY affected product. If a real enterprise product is co-affected, the CVE stays.

Core infrastructure (gateway / management / log server). Each CVE is tagged with the core network-security infrastructure it affects - the security GATEWAY (firewall/enforcement appliance), its central MANAGEMENT console, and the LOG SERVER (logging/analytics) - shown in the per-vendor sheets' "Affects Gateway / Mgmt / Log" column (filterable). Examples: Check Point Quantum Security Gateway / Security Management / Log Server. Palo Alto PAN-OS+Cloud NGFW / Panorama / Cortex Data Lake. Fortinet FortiOS+FortiProxy / FortiManager / FortiAnalyzer. Cisco Secure Firewall ASA+FTD / Management Center (FMC) / Secure Network Analytics. A CVE can affect more than one (e.g. "Gateway, Management"). The Dashboard's "Security gateway + management/log" bundle counts only these core-infrastructure CVEs per vendor. Endpoint, email, SIEM, NAC, sandbox and similar adjacent products are tracked but excluded from that bundle.

Vendor research in 3rd-party products. A CVE a vendor's CNA assigned for ANOTHER company's product (e.g. Check Point Research findings in Amazon Kindle, Philips Hue, Valve, WordPress plugins) is not that vendor's own product vulnerability and is dropped entirely (distinct from upstream-component CVEs below, which are listed but not counted).

Vendors compared. Seven vendors are tracked in the data store (CP, PAN, Fortinet, Cisco, Juniper, SonicWall, Sophos). The exported workbook is configurable. This report covers Check Point (CP), Palo Alto (PAN), Fortinet, and Cisco, in that order.

Time range. One sheet per vendor, 2020 through 2026 (the year is a column). The Dashboard aggregates interactively by bundle. A compact Summary sheet carries the Since-2021 High/Critical block (Summary!E20:F23) that external charts (the competitive slide) link to.

What Counts as a Tracked Vulnerability

Total vulnerabilities. Total = CVEs + any vendor-acknowledged vulnerabilities issued without a CVE. One row per CVE. Advisories listing several CVEs are split into separate rows so counts are accurate.

Vendor-managed SaaS. Cloud / vendor-managed services (Prisma Access, Cloud NGFW, Harmony SASE, etc.) ARE counted. Being SaaS means two things and no more: the fix equals the disclosure date (the vendor patches server-side, so there is no on-prem train to search), and the CVE is left out of the time-to-fix AVERAGE - a fix the customer never had to wait for or install is not a remediation window, so averaging it in as 1 day would flatter whichever vendor sells the most cloud. It is not an exclusion from the counts.

Cloud services that still ship customer-patched software. A cloud subscription usually also ships software the customer installs and must upgrade themselves: endpoint agents (Duo Authentication for Windows Logon, the Umbrella roaming client, the Harmony SASE Windows client, the ADEM agent), self-hosted consoles (Prisma Cloud Compute Edition), on-prem gateways (Duo Network Gateway) and CPE appliance software (Prisma SD-WAN ION, the Umbrella virtual appliance). Those are NOT treated as SaaS: the vendor publishes fixed versions and the customer carries the remediation window, so they count AND they are averaged. Only the parts the vendor patches server-side are flagged SaaS - judged per CVE from the advisory's affected-component list, not from the product's brand name.

Third-party CVEs. Vulnerabilities inherited from upstream components (e.g. OpenSSL, Log4j, curl, Apache, Linux kernel, ClamAV, Snort) are listed for completeness but NOT counted toward a vendor's totals or fix-time averages. They carry a non-vendor Source.

Exclusions. REJECTED CVEs (withdrawn / "not a vulnerability"), disputed CVEs ("** DISPUTED **"), "not impacted" notices, and out-of-scope/consumer products (above) are excluded from the data set.

Severity. Severity is the VENDOR's OWN published rating, not NVD's (they often differ). Check Point: the severity stated on its SK advisory. Palo Alto / Fortinet / Cisco: the vendor CVSS severity from their CNA feed (CVE-5.0 / CSAF). NVD's rating is used ONLY as a fallback when the vendor published none. The CVSS score is recorded separately for reference. Normalized to LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / CRITICAL.

Dates & Time-to-Fix

Disclosed date. The date the vulnerability became public: normally the vendor advisory/publish date. Where a credible public timeline shows the issue was reported to the vendor earlier (researcher disclosure write-up), that reported-to-vendor date is used instead and noted (see Original Report Date below).

Fix date. The date a patched build is available across the current major version AND the previous two (the three most recent supported major trains for the product family, e.g. PAN-OS in 2026 = 12.1, 11.2, 11.1). Only trains the CVE actually AFFECTS need a patch, and trains past end-of-engineering-support drop out of the required set.

Staggered patches. When fixes ship in waves across trains, the fix date is the date the LAST of the required trains is patched - the issue is not considered fixed until all are covered.

Migrate to a fixed release. When the vendor does NOT ship an in-train fix for an affected supported train but says "migrate to a fixed release" (move to a newer train), that train stays vulnerable until it leaves support. Its fix contribution is therefore its end-of-support date, and the overall fix is the latest of the in-train patches and that EoS date.

Multiple products. When a CVE affects several product families, the latest fixed-product-family date is used.

No fix date in the feed. Vendors publish fixed VERSIONS, not patch dates, so the automated feed often cannot date a fix. Resolution order: (1) a fix date carried from the prior curated workbook is used. (2) a CURRENT-YEAR CVE with no patch yet is projected as current date + 7 days (a growing estimate, flagged in the comment, that finalizes when a patch ships). (3) a PRIOR-YEAR CVE with no date from either source is left blank and surfaced in the missing-fixes report for an analyst/agent to source from the vendor advisory - it is NOT given a fabricated date that would distort averages.

Fix predating disclosure. If the patched version shipped before public disclosure (already fixed when disclosed, or an internally-found issue), the fix date is set equal to the disclosed date, giving the 1-day floor below.

Time to fix (days). Calendar days from disclosed date to fix date, with a floor of 1 - a same-day fix counts as 1 day, never 0, so same-day coordinated disclosures do not distort the data.

Known timeline. A vulnerability has a "known timeline" when there is a real fix duration (more than the 1-day floor). "Known timeline" averages exclude same-day/floor cases so they reflect only vulnerabilities with a measurable remediation gap.

What the averages leave out. Two things never enter a time-to-fix average, in either the known-timeline or the all-fixed basis: CVEs with no fix date at all (nothing to measure), and vendor-managed SaaS (server-side fix, so the 1 day is a definition rather than a wait). Everything else counted is averaged. Both filters apply identically to every vendor, Check Point included.

CISA KEV. The CISA KEV column is TRUE when the CVE appears in the U.S. CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog - i.e. there is reliable evidence the flaw has been exploited in the wild - and blank otherwise. It is informational (a real-world exploitation signal). It does not change whether a CVE is counted or how its fix date/severity are computed. Membership is refreshed from the CISA feed on every refresh. The Summary and Charts report the per-vendor counted KEV count and its average time-to-fix across ALL years (not year-windowed), since KEV entries include pre-2020 CVEs. A handful of KEV CVEs that predate the automated enumeration window are curated in from the catalog with their vendor-advisory disclosure/patch dates.

Original Report Date

Definition. Where the crediting researcher's write-up documents a disclosure timeline, the reported-to-vendor date is recorded in the Comment / Justification column and used as the disclosed date, giving the defensible reported-to-patched remediation window.

Default. Most CVEs are internal discoveries or coordinated same-day disclosures with no earlier public report date. For these the advisory/publish date stands (1-day floor).

Analyst corrections. Sourced analyst edits (Disclosed / Fix date / Severity / Comment / Link), made via the Correct... dialog or by importing an edited workbook, are the HIGHEST-precedence overlay and are re-applied on every refresh - manual fixes are never overwritten by automation. Every correction carries a comment and a source link, so it is auditable.

Notes & Caveats

Vendor self-rating. Because severity and "fixed in" data come from each vendor, cross-vendor comparison reflects differing disclosure and rating practices as much as underlying security. Read totals and averages with that in mind.

Comparison is editorial. These figures support analysis but do not by themselves rank vendor security. Human review is expected before any figure is published.
